title: Routing (React Router)
summary: **Routing** maps the browser URL to which components render, letting a single-page app feel like many pages. **React Router** is the de-facto library: `<Routes>` and `<Route>` declare the URL-to-component mapping, while hooks like `useParams` and `useNavigate` read and change the location.

subtopics.title: The SPA model and the History API
subtopics.explanation: A single-page app loads one HTML shell and then swaps components in and out as the URL changes, instead of requesting a fresh document per URL. Client-side routing achieves this with the browser History API: `pushState`/`replaceState` change the address bar and session history without a network round-trip, and the `popstate` event fires on back/forward so the router can re-match. Because navigation happens in place, in-memory state and scroll position are preserved. The catch: on a hard refresh of a deep URL the server must be configured to return the shell for any path, or you get a 404.

subtopics.title: Routes, Route, and Link
subtopics.explanation: `<Routes>` acts like a switch statement over the current URL, picking the best-matching `<Route>` and rendering its element, ranking more specific paths above looser ones. `<Link>` renders an anchor but intercepts the click to update the URL via the History API instead of triggering a server request. A `path="*"` route catches anything unmatched as a 404.
subtopics.example:
<Routes>
  <Route path="/" element={<Home />} />
  <Route path="/users/:id" element={<UserDetail />} />
  <Route path="*" element={<NotFound />} />
</Routes>

subtopics.title: Dynamic params (useParams)
subtopics.explanation: A dynamic segment like `:id` in a path is a placeholder that matches any value, and `useParams()` returns the parsed value inside the matched component. This powers master/detail screens where one route definition serves every record. Params always come back as strings and should be validated before use, since they come straight from an untrusted URL.

subtopics.title: Nested routes, layouts, and Outlet
subtopics.explanation: Child `<Route>`s nested under a parent share the parent's layout, which renders an `<Outlet/>` as the placeholder where the matched child appears. This lets shared chrome — nav, sidebar, headers — be written once and persist while only the inner content swaps. An index route (`<Route index>`) renders at the parent's exact path, and relative child links resolve against the parent so refactors are safer.
subtopics.example:
<Route path="/dash" element={<DashboardLayout />}>
  <Route index element={<Overview />} />
  <Route path="settings" element={<Settings />} />
</Route>

subtopics.title: Query params (useSearchParams)
subtopics.explanation: Search, filter, and pagination state belongs in the URL query string so it is shareable, bookmarkable, and survives a refresh. `useSearchParams` returns a getter/setter pair backed by the URL, working like a `URLSearchParams` you can read and update. Storing this state in the URL instead of component state means a pasted link reproduces the exact same view.

subtopics.title: Protected routes and redirects
subtopics.explanation: A route guard conditionally renders an `<Outlet/>` for authorized users or a `<Navigate>` redirect otherwise — but it is only a UX convenience, never real security, since authorization must still be enforced on the server. Two classic bugs: creating a `<Navigate>` element without returning it (so it never renders), and omitting the `replace` prop (so the protected URL lingers in history). Capturing the attempted location in navigation state lets you send the user back after login.

subtopics.title: Programmatic navigation (useNavigate)
subtopics.explanation: `useNavigate` returns a function to navigate from event handlers or effects rather than from a link click — for example redirecting after a successful form submit or login. Passing `{ replace: true }` swaps the current history entry instead of pushing a new one, which prevents the back button from returning to a now-irrelevant page like the login screen. Negative numbers navigate through history (`navigate(-1)` is back).
subtopics.example:
const navigate = useNavigate();
navigate('/dashboard', { replace: true });

subtopics.title: Lazy routes and data loaders
subtopics.explanation: Routes are the natural seam for code splitting: `React.lazy` plus a dynamic import wrapped in `<Suspense>` means users only download the code for the screen they visit, dramatically shrinking the initial bundle. Data routers add loaders that fetch at the route boundary in parallel with the lazy chunk, removing the render-then-fetch waterfall that `useEffect`-based fetching causes. Together they are among the cheapest, highest-impact performance wins in an SPA.
subtopics.example:
const Settings = React.lazy(() => import('./Settings'));
<Route path="settings" element={<Suspense fallback={<Spinner/>}><Settings/></Suspense>} />

foundations.overview: Routing is the system that decides which UI to show for a given URL. In a traditional website the server returns a fresh HTML page for every URL. A single-page application (SPA) loads one HTML shell and then JavaScript swaps the visible components in and out as the URL changes, without a full page reload. React Router is the library that wires the browser's URL to your React component tree.
foundations.formalDefinition: Client-side routing is the technique of intercepting URL changes in the browser (via the History API) and rendering different components in response, rather than requesting a new document from the server. React Router provides declarative components (`<BrowserRouter>`, `<Routes>`, `<Route>`, `<Link>`, `<Outlet>`) and hooks (`useParams`, `useNavigate`, `useLocation`, `useSearchParams`) to express and manipulate that mapping.
foundations.whyItMatters: Almost every non-trivial React app has more than one screen — a list, a detail view, a settings page. Routing gives each screen a real URL, so links are shareable, the back button works, and the app is bookmarkable and indexable. Without it you'd be hiding and showing things with state alone, losing all of those browser affordances.
foundations.mentalModel: Think of `<Routes>` as a switch statement over the current URL: React Router looks at the path, finds the best-matching `<Route>`, and renders its element. `<Link>` is just an anchor that updates the URL via the History API instead of triggering a server request. The URL becomes a piece of shared, addressable state.
foundations.browserPerspective: Client-side routing uses the browser History API (`pushState`/`replaceState`) to change the URL bar and add an entry to the session history without a network round-trip. The browser fires a `popstate` event on back/forward; React Router listens for it, reads `window.location`, and re-renders the matching route. The DOM is updated in place — no document reload, so scroll position and in-memory state can be preserved.
foundations.realWorldUsage: A dashboard with /users, /users/:id, and /settings; an e-commerce site with /products/:slug and a protected /checkout; a docs site with deeply nested section routes sharing a sidebar layout. Query params drive search and filters (e.g. /search?q=react&page=2).
foundations.businessImpact: Real URLs are essential for SEO, marketing links, analytics funnels, and customer support ('send me the link to that page'). Broken back-button behavior or unshareable URLs are a common source of user frustration and lost conversions.
foundations.engineeringImpact: A clear route table is a map of the whole app's surface area. Nested routes and layouts cut duplication, route-based code splitting keeps bundles small, and data routers/loaders move data fetching out of components and remove waterfalls.
foundations.performanceImpact: Lazy-loaded routes (React.lazy + dynamic import) mean users only download the code for the screen they visit, dramatically shrinking the initial bundle. Data router loaders can fetch in parallel with code loading, avoiding the render-then-fetch waterfall that useEffect-based fetching causes.
commonUseCases: Multi-screen apps with shareable, bookmarkable URLs
Shared layouts (nav + sidebar) with nested content via <Outlet>
Protected/authenticated areas behind a route guard
Search and filter state encoded in query params

commonMisconceptions.myth: Client-side routing changes the page the same way a normal link does.
commonMisconceptions.reality: A normal link makes the browser request a new document from the server. Client-side routing intercepts the click, updates the URL with the History API, and re-renders components in place — no full reload.

commonMisconceptions.myth: You need a routing library to have multiple 'pages' in React.
commonMisconceptions.reality: You can fake routing with state, but you lose real URLs, the back button, and bookmarking. A router restores all of those by syncing the URL with what renders.

commonMisconceptions.myth: Refreshing a deep client-side URL just works.
commonMisconceptions.reality: On a hard refresh the server receives the full path (e.g. /users/42) and must be configured to return the SPA shell for any path; otherwise you get a 404. This is why SPAs need a catch-all server rewrite.

visualExplorer.title: How a URL becomes the right screen
visualExplorer.caption: Walk through what happens from a link click to the matched component rendering — no server round-trip required.

steps.title: 1. User clicks a <Link>
steps.description: React Router intercepts the click and calls history.pushState to change the URL to /users/42, adding an entry to the browser's session history — no request is sent to the server.

steps.title: 2. The router reads the new location
steps.description: The router updates its internal location to /users/42 and notifies the React tree that the current path has changed.

steps.title: 3. <Routes> matches the path
steps.description: React Router scans its <Route> definitions and picks the best match for /users/:id, ranking more specific routes above looser ones.

steps.title: 4. Params are extracted
steps.description: The dynamic segment :id is parsed out, so useParams() returns { id: '42' } inside the matched component.

steps.title: 5. The matched element renders
steps.description: React renders the route's element (e.g. <UserDetail/>), and nested routes fill their parent's <Outlet>. Only the changed subtree updates the DOM.

steps.title: 6. Back button = popstate
steps.description: Pressing back fires a popstate event; the router reads window.location, re-matches, and renders the previous screen — all without a page reload.

interactiveExamples.title: A runnable mini hash router (the core idea)
interactiveExamples.explanation: React Router isn't loaded in this sandbox, so this demonstrates the underlying concept with plain React: the URL hash is the 'location', and a switch over it decides what renders. Clicking a link changes window.location.hash; a hashchange listener updates state and re-renders. This is exactly what a real router does, minus the History API and matching engine.
interactiveExamples.expectedOutput: A nav with three links. Clicking them changes the heading and the 'current path' line without any page reload; the browser back button also works.

interactiveExamples.explanation: This is how you'd write the previous demo with the real library. It will NOT run in this sandbox because react-router-dom isn't loaded here — it is shown to illustrate the real API. <BrowserRouter> provides routing context, <Routes>/<Route> declare the mapping, <Link> navigates, and useParams reads the dynamic :id segment.

interactiveExamples.explanation: Nested <Route> elements share a parent layout. The parent renders an <Outlet> where the matched child appears, so the nav/sidebar is written once. Index routes render at the parent's exact path. This snippet is illustrative — react-router-dom is not loaded here.

codeLab.title: Build a custom hash router with a useNavigate-style helper
codeLab.instructions: Extend the runnable mini-router. Add a 'Go to User 7' button that navigates programmatically by setting window.location.hash (the concept behind useNavigate). The button should NOT be an <a> tag — it must navigate from a click handler. Render Home at '/', and 'User #N' for '/users/N'.
codeLab.expectedOutput: Clicking the button changes the URL hash and renders 'User #7' without a reload.
hints: useNavigate's equivalent here is just setting window.location.hash inside an onClick handler.
Parse the dynamic id with path.split('/')[2] for '/users/7'.
The hashchange listener already re-renders when the hash changes, so the handler only needs to set the hash.

debuggingLab.title: The protected route that lets everyone in
debuggingLab.symptom: An unauthenticated user can still reach /dashboard even though there's a guard.
debuggingLab.errorAnalysis: Two bugs. First, the condition is inverted: it redirects when the user IS logged in. Second, and more importantly, <Navigate /> is created but never returned, so React never renders it and the redirect never happens — the function falls through to <Outlet /> for everyone.
commonMistakes: Inverting the auth condition (guarding the wrong branch).
Creating a <Navigate /> element without returning it — JSX has no effect unless rendered.
Forgetting the `replace` prop, leaving the protected URL in history so back returns to it.
debuggingLab.fixChallenge: Return <Navigate to="/login" replace /> when the user is NOT logged in, otherwise return <Outlet />.

theory.question: What is client-side routing and how does it differ from traditional server-side routing?
theory.directAnswer: Client-side routing intercepts URL changes in the browser and renders different components in place using the History API, without requesting a new document from the server. Server-side routing returns a fresh HTML page for every URL. A single-page app loads one shell and swaps components as the URL changes, so navigation feels instant and in-app state is preserved.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: A way to map the browser URL to UI entirely on the client, so the app feels like multiple pages while only ever loading one document.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: It removes the full-page reload between screens, keeping navigation fast and preserving in-memory state, while still giving each screen a real, shareable URL.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: A router listens for URL changes (link clicks intercepted, plus the popstate event), uses pushState/replaceState to update the address bar, matches the path against a route table, and renders the matching component subtree.

theory.whyImportant: Understanding the SPA model explains why deep links need a server catch-all, why the back button can break if you misuse navigation, and why routing libraries exist at all.
theory.realWorldExample: Gmail changes the URL as you open a conversation, but the page never reloads — labels, search, and the sidebar stay mounted while the reading pane swaps.

nestedTopics.title: History API
nestedTopics.explanation: pushState/replaceState change the URL and history stack without a request; popstate fires on back/forward.

nestedTopics.title: The SPA shell
nestedTopics.explanation: One HTML file boots the JS app; the server must serve it for all client routes so deep links and refreshes work.

nestedTopics.title: Hash vs browser history
nestedTopics.explanation: Hash routing (#/path) needs no server config but uglier URLs; browser/history routing has clean URLs but requires a server rewrite.

followUps.question: Why does refreshing /users/42 sometimes 404?
followUps.answer: On a hard refresh the server gets the full path and, unless configured to return the SPA shell for any path, has nothing to serve. A catch-all rewrite fixes it.

followUps.question: Does client-side routing hurt SEO?
followUps.answer: It can, because crawlers may see an empty shell. Server-side rendering or static pre-rendering (e.g. with a framework) addresses this.

theory.question: Explain nested routes, layouts, and the <Outlet> component in React Router.
theory.directAnswer: Nested routes let a parent <Route> wrap child routes that share its layout. The parent renders an <Outlet/>, which is the placeholder where the matched child route's element appears. This means shared chrome — nav, sidebar, headers — is written once in the parent and persists while only the inner content changes. An index route renders at the parent's exact path.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: A tree of routes where parents provide layout and an <Outlet/>, and children fill that outlet based on the matched URL segment.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: To eliminate duplication of shared layout across many screens and to model the natural hierarchy of an app (e.g. /dashboard owns /dashboard/settings).
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: React Router matches the full path against the nested tree, rendering each matched level and substituting its child into the parent's <Outlet/>. Relative paths in children resolve against the parent path.

theory.whyImportant: Layouts and Outlet are the idiomatic way to structure real apps; interviewers use them to check you can model hierarchy rather than repeating navigation in every page.
theory.realWorldExample: A settings area at /settings with a left menu; /settings/profile and /settings/billing swap in the right pane via <Outlet/> while the menu stays put.

nestedTopics.title: Index routes
nestedTopics.explanation: <Route index> renders when the URL exactly matches the parent path, e.g. the default view of /dashboard.

nestedTopics.title: Relative links
nestedTopics.explanation: Inside a nested route, <Link to="settings"> resolves relative to the parent path, so refactors are safer.

nestedTopics.title: Multiple outlets vs one
nestedTopics.explanation: Each layout level has its own single Outlet; deeply nested UIs compose layouts rather than using many outlets at once.

followUps.question: How do you share data between a layout and its children?
followUps.answer: Outlet supports a `context` prop; children read it with useOutletContext(). Or lift state to the layout and pass via context/props.

followUps.question: What renders if no child matches under a layout?
followUps.answer: Add an index route for the default and a path="*" catch-all for unknown nested paths.

scenario.question: After logging in, your users land back on the login page instead of the page they were trying to reach. How do you design the redirect so they return to their original destination?
scenario.directAnswer: When the guard redirects an unauthenticated user to /login, capture the location they were trying to reach and pass it in navigation state: <Navigate to="/login" replace state={{ from: location }} />. After a successful login, read that state with useLocation and navigate(from, { replace: true }), defaulting to a safe page if it's absent.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: A 'return-to' redirect pattern where the protected route remembers the intended destination through the login flow.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Sending everyone to a fixed landing page after login is jarring and loses the user's intent — especially for deep links shared in email.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: The guard stores the attempted location in router state during the redirect. The login screen reads location.state.from on success and navigates there with replace, so the login page isn't left in history.

scenario.whyImportant: It tests practical use of useLocation, useNavigate, navigation state, and the `replace` option — and an understanding of the history stack.

nestedTopics.title: replace vs push
nestedTopics.explanation: replace swaps the current history entry so back doesn't return to the login or protected URL.

nestedTopics.title: Navigation state
nestedTopics.explanation: The state object travels with the navigation and is read via useLocation().state; it isn't visible in the URL.

followUps.question: What if `from` is missing?
followUps.answer: Default to a safe route like '/' or '/dashboard' so the flow never breaks.

followUps.question: Why use replace on the post-login navigate?
followUps.answer: So pressing back doesn't bounce the now-authenticated user back onto the login page.

coding.question: Implement a tiny client-side router from scratch (no library) that supports a static route and a dynamic /users/:id route, using the URL hash as the location.
coding.thoughtProcess: A router needs three things: read the current location, re-render when it changes, and match the location to a component. I'll read window.location.hash for the location, subscribe to the hashchange event in useEffect to re-render, and write a small matcher: exact match for static paths, prefix match plus a split for the dynamic segment to extract the param.
coding.lineByLine: useHashRoute reads the initial hash lazily and subscribes to hashchange, cleaning up on unmount to avoid leaks. The matcher checks exact '/', then a prefix for '/users/' and extracts the id via split. go(to) returns a click handler that sets the hash, which fires hashchange and triggers a re-render — mirroring useNavigate.
coding.timeComplexity: O(1) per navigation for matching this fixed route set.
coding.spaceComplexity: O(1) — only the current path string is stored.

alternativeApproaches.title: History API instead of hash
alternativeApproaches.explanation: Use pushState and listen for popstate for clean URLs, but you must intercept link clicks and configure a server catch-all so refreshes don't 404.

alternativeApproaches.title: A route table with regex
alternativeApproaches.explanation: Compile each route pattern to a regex with named groups so matching and param extraction generalize beyond hard-coded checks — this is closer to what real routers do.

followUps.question: How would you add a programmatic redirect?
followUps.answer: Set window.location.hash inside an effect or handler — e.g. redirect to '/login' when not authenticated — which is the hash-router analog of <Navigate>.

followUps.question: How do query params fit in?
followUps.answer: Parse them from the location string with URLSearchParams; in React Router you'd use useSearchParams which gives a getter/setter pair backed by the URL.

productionDeepDive.architecture: Define routes as a single declarative tree (or a data router route object array) that mirrors the app's hierarchy: top-level layout, feature sections, and detail routes with dynamic params. Co-locate route definitions with features, and use nested layouts so shared chrome lives in one place. Prefer data routers/loaders to move fetching to the route boundary and out of components.
productionDeepDive.performance: Code-split at route boundaries with React.lazy + dynamic import and wrap in <Suspense> so the initial bundle only contains the shell and the first screen. With data routers, loaders fetch in parallel with the lazy chunk, removing the render-then-fetch waterfall. Prefetch likely-next routes on link hover for instant transitions.
productionDeepDive.security: Route guards are a UX convenience, not real security — they only hide UI. Always enforce authorization on the server for the underlying data and APIs. Never trust client-side params; validate :id and query values before using them. Use `replace` on auth redirects so protected URLs don't linger in history.
productionDeepDive.scaling: As route counts grow, group routes by feature and split bundles per section to keep build and load times bounded. A data-router route config (objects rather than JSX) scales better for large apps and enables centralized loaders, error boundaries, and type-safe params.
productionDeepDive.maintainability: Use relative links inside nested routes so moving a section doesn't break links. Centralize path strings or generate them from the route config to avoid magic strings scattered across the app. Add a catch-all 404 route and per-route error boundaries.
productionDeepDive.observability: Track route changes for analytics by listening to location changes (e.g. a useEffect on useLocation) and reporting page views. Surface route-level errors via errorElement/error boundaries and log the failing path and params.

caseStudies.problem: Initial bundle ballooned because every screen was imported eagerly, slowing first load.
caseStudies.solution: Switched to route-based code splitting with React.lazy and Suspense fallbacks per section.
caseStudies.tradeoffs: A brief loading state on first visit to a new section vs a far smaller initial download.
caseStudies.lessons: Routes are the natural seam for code splitting; lazy-loading per route is one of the cheapest, highest-impact performance wins.

caseStudies.problem: Deep links into protected pages dumped users on a generic landing page after login, losing their intent.
caseStudies.solution: The guard recorded the attempted location in navigation state and the login flow redirected back to it with replace.
caseStudies.tradeoffs: A little extra state plumbing vs a much smoother, intent-preserving login.
caseStudies.lessons: Treat the URL as the source of truth for intent and carry it through cross-cutting flows like auth.

projectBuilder.summary: Add multi-screen navigation to the dashboard: a users list, a user detail page with a dynamic param, a shared layout with a sidebar, and a protected settings area — modeled with React Router (or the runnable hash-router concept).
requirements: A persistent layout with a sidebar and an <Outlet> for content
Routes for /users (list) and /users/:id (detail) using a dynamic param
A protected /settings route behind an auth guard
A search query stored in the URL via query params
projectBuilder.architecture: A root layout route renders the sidebar and an Outlet. Child routes cover the users list, the user detail (reading :id with useParams), and a guarded settings route. Search state lives in the URL via useSearchParams so it's shareable and survives refresh.
projectBuilder.folderStructure:
src/
  routes/
    AppLayout.jsx
    UsersList.jsx
    UserDetail.jsx
    Settings.jsx
    RequireAuth.jsx
  App.jsx

steps.title: Set up the route tree
steps.instructions: Wrap the app in a router and declare a layout route with nested child routes for /users and /settings.
steps.checkpoint: Navigating between sections swaps the content while the sidebar stays.

steps.title: Add the dynamic detail route
steps.instructions: Create /users/:id and read the id with useParams to show that user's details.
steps.checkpoint: Clicking a user opens /users/:id and shows the right record.

steps.title: Protect settings
steps.instructions: Add a RequireAuth guard that redirects unauthenticated users to /login with replace, returning <Outlet/> when allowed.
steps.checkpoint: Logged-out users can't reach /settings and bounce to login.

steps.title: Put search in the URL
steps.instructions: Use useSearchParams (or parse the hash) to store the list's search query so it's bookmarkable.
steps.checkpoint: Reloading the page keeps the search term and results.

enhancements: Lazy-load each section with React.lazy + Suspense
Add a data-router loader to fetch the user before the detail route renders
Show a 404 route for unknown paths
interviewQuestions: Why store the search query in the URL instead of component state?
How would you preserve the intended destination through the login redirect?
Where would you put data loading to avoid a render-then-fetch waterfall?

keyTakeaways: Client-side routing maps the URL to components in place via the History API — no server round-trip per navigation.
<Routes>/<Route> declare the mapping; <Link> navigates, useNavigate navigates programmatically, useParams reads dynamic segments.
Nested routes plus <Outlet> let layouts (nav, sidebar) be written once and persist while inner content changes.
Route guards only hide UI — enforce real authorization on the server, and use `replace` so protected URLs don't linger in history.
Lazy-load routes and use data-router loaders to shrink bundles and avoid render-then-fetch waterfalls.
